items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: he is also the closest thing I’ve heard to say Clifford Brown

ctx.x: I’m sorry, the younger white musicians?

The younger black musicians, did I say white? The younger black musicians don’t know the origins of jazz and they don’t know say the New Orleans tradition except for those who are down in New Orleans. A great example of the positive side of a young black musician knowing the foundation of the music is Nicholas Payton. I consider Nicholas to be the outstanding young jazz musician in the world today, by a considerable margin, and one reason is that he not only knows the music from the beginning on, but he can play…
goodness, and that was the duet album with Doc Cheatham and the performance of “Stardust.” I can’t even talk about it.

items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: or he saw Brownie and Max talking to me or something

ctx.x: All right. We will later. If not, I’ll make a tape and send it to you. Her great favorite musician is Sonny Rollins. She fell in love, when she was a little girl, with the track, If Ever You Should Leave Me [If Ever I Would Leave You] on the first Sonny Rollins album, The Bridge, which of course was called The Bridge because I had the idea of signing Sonny when he came out of retirement, where he was heard playing in the upper reaches of the Williamsburg Bridge among the cable wires and all. I thought, gee, Sonny…

with Mercury. But Sonny I guess might have known who I was or something, or he saw Brownie and Max talking to me or something, and somehow, each time I went, there would be a time during the evening when Sonny would sit, during the intermission. We’d just talk. I found that he was a much more interesting person than just the average musician. That made it very easy, when I decided to go after a contract with him, to talk with him. The contract, by the way, was done in an unusual way – not as unusual as the Miles…
